catalog_quote: Kisa, a Bantu language spoken in Western Kenya, portrays a mixed system of tone and stress. ... The findings show that Kisa exhibits linguistic stress patterns that are weight sensitive. There is one primary stress per word; primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable or the rightmost heavy syllable in a word. Secondary stress falls on the left mora in a foot marked from the right to the left of the word. The findings attest to the fact that Kisa portrays a mixed system of stress and tone. But because tone height and vowel duration do not always co-occur and in Kisa and that Kisa portrays a weight sensitive stress system, duration is the primary phonetic correlate of stress in this language, even though loudness and pitch are also correlates of stress in Kisa.

The <jats:p> abstract contains the reported passage word for word, from 'The findings show that Kisa exhibits linguistic stress patterns that are weight sensitive. There is one primary stress per word; primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable or the rightmost heavy syllable in a word. Secondary stress falls on the left mora in a foot marked from the right to the left of the word.' through '..even though loudness and pitch are also correlates of stress…
new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary stress per word: default penultimate syllable, but a heavy (long-vowel) syllable attracts it -- stress goes to the rightmost heavy syllable, else the penult. Kisa is also a tone language (H vs default L), so this is a stress statement for a tonal Bantu lect; duration is named as the main stress correlate.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the left (first) mora of each foot, feet built right-to-left from the primary stress (per abstract).
new_statements.exceptions: None visible in the abstract; interaction of 'rightmost heavy' with the penult default (e.g. heavy antepenult vs light penult, final syllables never long since word-final long vowels are banned per Ondondo 2013:58-61) can only be checked in the body text.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level ('one primary stress per word'); OT analysis based on data from two native speakers plus the author. Whether forms are citation/isolation forms is not stated in the abstract.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Kisa proper (kisa1263), the Luhya lect of Khwisero, Western Kenya; Ondondo is a native speaker. Sample 1976 uses the name 'Olukisa', Donohew 1973 'Shisa' -- same lect.
